questions.question: For the Proxima Bank 429 spike after priority routing rollout, what caused the throttling and what temporary policy exception did we apply, and how do we verify it is not burning the enterprise route SLOs?
questions.answer: Throttling was triggered by hot-route protection admission control in us-east: Proxima's bursty combined chat+embeddings traffic exceeded the conservative enterprise route-group burst/budget during a regional pressure window (elevated queue depth/scheduler lag), so requests were denied as "overload_protection_admission/admission_over_budget" with Retry-After 1-2s (not primarily quota). We applied a temporary, region-scoped policy override for PROXIMA-ENT-014: increased the burst multiplier/budget for chat+embeddings in us-east only, time-boxed for 14 days with guardrails/auto-rollback. To verify it's not burning enterprise route SLOs, watch the enterprise (Protected) route x region dashboards for chat/completions and embeddings: error-budget burn/availability and p95/p99 latency stay within SLO targets, 5xx stays below burn thresholds, and enterprise overload/admission-control 429s (which count against enterprise availability) plus enterprise shed_rate remain near zero (alert-level if sustained).
facts: The 429 throttling was triggered by hot-route protection admission control in us-east.
Proxima bursty combined chat and embeddings traffic exceeded the enterprise route-group burst or budget during a regional pressure window (elevated queue depth or scheduler lag).
Requests were denied with reason overload_protection_admission/admission_over_budget and included a Retry-After of 1 to 2 seconds.
The throttling was not primarily caused by quota limits.
A temporary region-scoped policy override was applied for PROXIMA-ENT-014 to increase the burst multiplier or budget for chat and embeddings in us-east only.
The override was time-boxed for 14 days and included guardrails or auto-rollback.
To verify the exception is not burning enterprise route SLOs, monitor enterprise protected route by-region dashboards for chat/completions and embeddings.
Verify enterprise error-budget burn or availability and p95 or p99 latency remain within SLO targets.
Verify 5xx rates stay below burn thresholds.
Verify enterprise overload or admission-control 429s and enterprise shed_rate remain near zero (alert if sustained).

questions.question: What is the procedure for an emergency rollback of a Serving Runtime release (Hosted and Dedicated)?
questions.answer: For an emergency rollback of a Serving Runtime release in Hosted and Dedicated, first pause/freeze any in-flight progressive rollout so it cannot auto-advance, then re-pin the runtime to a known-good prior runtime release tag, trigger a redeploy, and verify fleet health (e.g., 5xx rate, p95 TTFT, GPU OOMs) before closing the incident/change record. For Hosted, apply the rollback across regions in order (non-critical/canary first, then remaining canary, then all affected regions) and lock the tag to prevent re-advance; for Dedicated, identify impacted tenant clusters, pin and redeploy per cluster (coordinating customer comms as required), and keep the incident open until metrics are stable (≈30 minutes Hosted, ≈60 minutes Dedicated) while capturing CI/CD job links, affected regions/clusters, tags, timings, and verification evidence.
facts: In an emergency rollback of a Serving Runtime release, first pause or freeze any in-flight progressive rollout so it cannot auto-advance.
Re-pin the serving runtime to a known-good prior runtime release tag.
Trigger a redeploy after re-pinning the runtime tag.
Verify fleet health after the rollback using metrics such as 5xx rate, p95 TTFT, and GPU OOMs.
Close the incident or change record only after verification is complete.
For Hosted, apply the rollback across regions in order: non-critical or canary first, then remaining canary, then all affected regions.
For Hosted, lock the runtime tag to prevent re-advance after rollback.
For Dedicated, identify the impacted tenant clusters.
For Dedicated, pin and redeploy per impacted tenant cluster.
For Dedicated, coordinate customer communications as required during the rollback.
Keep the incident open until metrics are stable, approximately 30 minutes for Hosted and approximately 60 minutes for Dedicated.
Capture incident evidence including CI/CD job links, affected regions or clusters, runtime tags, timings, and verification evidence.

questions.question: In the planned controlled failover game day on 2026-01-15 (Hosted API us-east → eu-west), what caused the routing automation to oscillate (flip/rollback), and what follow-up ticket and target ship date were created to fix the streaming disconnect/reconnect behavior clients saw during cross-region redirects?
questions.answer: The flip/rollback oscillation was caused by noisy/false-positive reachability health signals (including a premature "recovery" signal) combined with overly permissive hold-down/anti-flap and rollback guardrails, letting the controller fail over and then roll back repeatedly. The streaming redirect disconnect/reconnect follow-up was ticket ENG-2422, targeting a production ship (behind a flag) by 2026-02-07.
facts: The routing automation oscillation (flip/rollback) was caused by noisy or false-positive reachability health signals, including a premature recovery signal.
The routing automation oscillation was also enabled by overly permissive hold-down or anti-flap and rollback guardrails, which allowed repeated failover and rollback.
The follow-up ticket created to fix the streaming redirect disconnect/reconnect behavior was ENG-2422.
The target ship date for the ENG-2422 fix was 2026-02-07 (production ship behind a flag).
The answer must not attribute the event to the 2025-02-19 us-east-1 incident or a failover to us-west-2 (different date and regions).
The answer must not claim the streaming issue was an SSE stall/freeze mid-response fixed by upgrading to runtime 2.18.3; that is a different known issue than cross-region redirect reconnect.
The answer must not name ENG-2426 as the specific follow-up ticket for the streaming redirect reconnect fix; ENG-2426 is an action-item tracker, not the ticket called out for that fix.
The answer must not give 2026-02-28 as the target ship date for the streaming redirect reconnect fix; the game day follow-up ticket specifies 2026-02-07.
The answer must not cite SUP-25310 (support macro for transient 5xx) as the engineering follow-up ticket to fix streaming reconnect behavior.

The answer must not describe the resolution as a manual traffic shift/weight change procedure from the manual failover runbook; the question asks what caused automation oscillation and the specific follow-up ticket/date.
